archetype.name: Improviser
archetype.definition: A veteran who holds the ball looking for something downfield or a lane to run, living with sacks to make out-of-structure plays and to find the intermediate and deep throws that carry his passing value.

report.headline: Productive between the 20s, but the sacks and missing touchdowns cap the ceiling
report.take:
Watson in 2026 is the most functional Cleveland version of himself we have seen, though not the Houston one. His passing EPA per dropback of -0.016 ranks 28th of 55, a little above the league-average mark of -0.027. His 7.33 yards per attempt and 235.3 yards a game sit in the top third. The Houston seasons, with EPA per play between 0.15 and 0.22 and a CPOE consistently above +2, are gone. His -0.83 CPOE now ranks 28th. What remains is a quarterback who extends plays, scrambles well, and gets most of his value from throws past 10 yards.

The passing value is lopsided. On throws of 10+ air yards he averages 0.402 EPA, with the intermediate band at 0.361 and deep shots at 0.46. Underneath 10 yards he is close to zero at 0.012, and throws behind the line are negative with a -9.1 CPOE. His tight end, Harold Fannin Jr., is the engine at 0.342 EPA per target, far ahead of any wideout. The cost of all this is the sack rate: 11.3% of dropbacks, 47th of 55, with 41.6% of pressures ending in a sack. The line shares the blame, since Cleveland's offense allows the highest hit rate in the league (32nd of 32). But a high pressure-to-sack rate has followed him for years: 54.1% in 2022 and 37.9% in 2024. Both he and the line are causes.

The raw numbers hide a style shift. Over the last three games he has thrown for 314.7 yards a game at 8.21 yards per attempt, going over 300 three straight times. His aggressiveness collapsed in the same stretch, to 5.6%, 5.1% and 7.5% tight-window rates after sitting in the high teens early. So the yardage is coming from more volume and more completions, not from more ambition. Over that stretch he threw zero touchdowns, and EPA per dropback (-0.018) barely moved. The 2.4% touchdown rate ranks 45th, and his red-zone (-0.049) and third-down (-0.146) EPA are both negative. Drives stall where the field shrinks and the sacks bite hardest.

Going forward, the yards and the legs look real. The touchdown drought should partly correct, because a 0% TD rate over 115 attempts is too low for a passer this productive between the 20s. The sacks and fumbles are structural and will keep a lid on his efficiency. His availability needs watching: he sat Week 9 after a limited week, came back to play every snap in Week 10, and is listed QB1 on the depth chart, but the site carries him as Out.

strengths.title: Real value past the sticks
strengths.body: Almost all of his passing EPA comes on throws of 10+ air yards, where he is efficient despite completing fewer than half of them. Short of 10 yards he is close to break-even. This matches his career: even in Cleveland his aDOT has sat in the 7-9 range with steady aggressiveness. The recent move toward safer throws risks giving some of it up.

strengths.title: Scrambling pays the bills
strengths.body: His 26 scrambles average 0.31 EPA and produced 10 first downs, and his 29.6 rushing yards a game rank 3rd among quarterbacks. Designed runs are a different story: -0.191 EPA with no explosives, so the value comes from improvising, not from called keepers. He has been a top-tier rushing quarterback in most seasons of his career, so this should hold.

strengths.title: Keeps the ball out of coverage
strengths.body: His 1.4% interception rate ranks 15th and sits well under the league's 2.5%. That is notable given how often he is under duress and how long he holds the ball. Some of it comes from the recent conservatism, but he has not been reckless at any point this season.

concerns.title: Sacks are the tax on everything
concerns.body: An 11.3% sack rate (47th) and a 41.6% pressure-to-sack rate (41st of 45) drain drives, especially on third down, where 13 sacks feed a -0.146 EPA. The worst hit rate in the league says the line is part of it. His career pressure-to-sack numbers say holding the ball is part of it too. Expect this to persist.

concerns.title: Yards without touchdowns
concerns.body: His 2.4% TD rate ranks 45th, and he threw none across the last three games despite 314.7 yards a game. Red-zone passing is slightly negative, and the recent shift away from tight-window throws makes him easier to defend on a compressed field. Some of this is small-sample bad luck that should ease. The red-zone and third-down struggles are a real ceiling, though.

concerns.title: Ball security in the pocket
concerns.body: Three lost fumbles rank 51st of 55, and charting has eight turnover-worthy fumbles. That is the other side of holding the ball and taking hits. It tracks with the sack volume, so it is unlikely to clean up on its own.

trend.note: Game EPA has swung from +7.6 and +7.4 in September to -10.4 against the Jets. The last three games brought big yardage but flat efficiency and no passing touchdowns, as aggressiveness fell into single digits.

nextGame.headline: A leaky Raiders pass defense with a thinned interior line
nextGame.body:
Las Vegas ranks 28th in pass EPA allowed and last in success rate. It is also worst in the league on short throws (0.226 EPA), the exact area where Watson has been break-even, so the underneath game should finally produce. Quarterbacks score 19.2 PPR a game against this defense (28th), and it allows 2.36 passing touchdowns a game (31st). That is a real chance to end the drought. The Raiders' pressure is middling, with a sack rate ranked 16th, which matters a lot for a quarterback whose biggest leak is sacks. Cleveland is favored by 4.5 with a 41.5 total.

Availability matters on both sides. Raiders interior lineman Tonka Hemingway is out, and three more defensive tackles (Butler, Keenan, Pegues) are questionable after leaving the last game. A depleted interior should mean fewer quick pressures up the middle and cleaner pockets to step into. On Cleveland's side, the question is Watson himself. He is listed QB1 and played every snap in Week 10, but the site status reads Out, so confirm before kickoff. Only a backup fullback is on the Browns' report.

keyMatchups.title: Short game vs worst short defense
keyMatchups.body: Watson's under-10 throws have produced almost nothing all year, while Las Vegas allows the most EPA in the league on short passes. If the check-down-heavy approach of the last three games continues, this is the opponent where it should turn into efficiency rather than empty yardage.

keyMatchups.title: Fannin into a tougher spot
keyMatchups.body: Fannin is his most efficient target by a wide margin. The Raiders have held lead tight ends slightly under their averages, ranking 11th by EPA allowed to the role. The soft spot is the secondary receiver: Las Vegas ranks 32nd against WR2s by both points over average and EPA. That could tilt targets toward Boston or Concepcion.

keyMatchups.title: Depleted Raiders interior line
keyMatchups.body: With Hemingway out and several defensive tackles questionable, interior push should be lighter. That is the pressure that most often turns his long-hold dropbacks into sacks. A clean middle also opens his scramble lanes, where he has been efficient.

nextGame.watch: Whether he takes his shots again: an aggressiveness rate back near the teens would signal the touchdowns are coming back, not just more 300-yard games built on check-downs.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume looks durable. Cleveland passes a bit more than expected (11th), he is averaging 32.1 attempts, and the recent run of 38-40 attempt games has pushed his yardage up. Rushing should stay a steady floor of roughly 20-35 yards with occasional short touchdowns, since the scrambles are a career-long skill. I project 240-290 passing yards a game. Touchdowns should drift up toward one a game, because a passer this productive between the 20s rarely stays near the bottom in TD rate, though I'd stop short of 1.5.

The efficiency should stay roughly where it is: near league average per dropback, held down by a sack rate that is both scheme-driven and a career trait. Expect four or so sacks a game and the occasional strip. The swing is whether he recovers his willingness to throw intermediate and deep, where his value actually lives, or settles into a high-completion, low-yield style.

confidence.note: Nine starts of consistent sack and depth patterns, but his availability is uncertain and his style shifted over the last three games.
